# MCP Apps and A2UI: The Two Architectures That Will Define Generative UI for Enterprise AI Agents


[Workday Technology Writer](https://medium.com/@workday_technology?source=post_page---byline--f22175863037-----------------------------------------)

*By Samuel Weick, Principal Product Manager at Workday*


If you build agents for systems of record, you’ve felt this tension: models move fast, UX patterns are evolving under your feet, and every new “AI canvas” demo ships with an implicit question no one answers, *what is the actual contract between the agent and the UI?* In most stacks, that contract is still an afterthought. The agent spits out text or JSON, the client hacks together some cards or widgets, and you hope nothing mission critical depends on it. That won’t fly when the agent sits on top of HR, Finance, and IT systems where the margin for error is effectively zero.


Generative UI is the bridge. It’s how we let agents compose interfaces dynamically, grounded in trusted components, governed data, and existing controls, rather than hard coding every screen in advance. And today, two emerging open specifications are starting to define how that bridge actually works: Anthropic’s MCP Apps and Google’s A2UI.


They represent two very different answers to a core question: **who controls the palette, and who holds the brush?** This piece is about those tradeoffs, from the perspective of teams building durable agentic systems in enterprise environments like Workday.


## **TL;DR**


Generative UI is moving from “cool demo widgets” to the surface where agents do work:


- MCP Apps lets servers ship full embedded web apps into agent hosts: maximum expressiveness, heavier trust and governance surface.
- A2UI has agents emit declarative JSON that the client renders with its own components: maximum safety and visual consistency, constrained expressiveness.
- In enterprise settings like Workday, the right architecture depends on trust: who owns the UI, what systems of record are in play, and which governance rails you’re required to stay on.
- Most serious stacks will land on a hybrid: a curated component palette for 90% of workflows, and deeply vetted embedded apps where full fidelity partner experiences matter.
- The “agent canvas” is the pattern where all of this comes together, a persistent, governed workspace where agents and humans co‑create, not just chat.


If you’re a staff engineer thinking about where to invest, this is the shape of the platform you’re going to be building against.


## **From Static Screens to a Generative Palette**


When you hand a painter a canvas, they don’t manufacture pigments mid stroke. They start from a palette: a curated, deliberate set of colors and tools. The painting is generative; the palette is not. Enterprise software already works this way in one important sense. Strong product teams build design systems: reusable components, design tokens, accessibility patterns, interaction rules, and data contracts. Engineers don’t need to reinvent a button, table, or approval control for every screen. What has traditionally been fixed though, is the **composition** . Designers decide in advance which components belong on a given page. Engineers encode those layouts and workflows. PMs define the states and acceptance criteria. QA verifies that the resulting experience behaves predictably. The system is deliberately deterministic: for a known task, a known screen appears in a known way. That model produces reliable software. But it also means the interface is optimized for the workflows we anticipated at the design time. It can struggle when a user’s need cuts across those predefined screens, data models, and process boundaries.


When a controller asks, “Where are my renewal risks this quarter?” they don’t need a paragraph of text or a journey through five pre-built reports. They need an interactive workspace composed from trusted elements: a renewal risk chart, a contracts table, policy context, and actions appropriate to their permissions. When an HRBP asks, “Help me prepare this reorg,” they don’t want a blob of natural language; they need an organization’s view, headcount and compensation summaries, scenario comparisons, and the right review or approval action. Generative UI does not replace the design system. It makes the design system available to an agent at runtime


The **palette remains curated** : the components, governed data, interaction patterns, security boundaries, and deterministic workflows. What becomes dynamic is the agent’s ability to compose those trusted pieces into an interface that fits the user, task, and moment. You could pre-build every possible screen for every combination of intent. But you’ll drown on day two.

If you work on something like Workday Agent Factory, this isn’t an abstract idea. This is what we’re building against it. The open question is: *what’s the right architecture to make that contract explicit and durable?* Two serious answers have emerged to standardize how agents summon UI at runtime, and they represent different philosophies.


## **MCP Apps: Letting Partners Bring Their Whole UI**


[https://github.com/MCP-UI-Org/mcp-ui](https://github.com/MCP-UI-Org/mcp-ui)


MCP Apps, formalized as SEP-1865 and co-authored by maintainers at Anthropic and OpenAI, extends the Model Context Protocol with a standardized pattern for serving interactive user interfaces from MCP servers.


At a mechanical level, it’s straightforward:


- Servers declare UI resources using a ui:// URI scheme.
- Those resources are linked to tools through metadata.
- When invoked, the server returns real HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
- The host (Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose, etc.) renders that payload in a sandboxed iframe and brokers communication via JSON‑RPC over postMessage.


Conceptually, this is a **“mini web app”** model. The server shows up with its own paints and brushes. The host provides wall space, security boundaries, and a message bus. The upside is obvious if you’ve ever tried to port a complex app into a new component model:


- There’s effectively no ceiling on expressiveness. If Canva wants to bring a full design editor, or a data platform wants to expose a live notebook, MCP Apps is a natural fit.
- Third‑party vendors don’t have to rebuild frontends for each agent host; they can reuse their existing investments and ship a consistent experience across surfaces.


For Workday adjacent scenarios, this is compelling when you want rich, recognizable experiences from deeply trusted partners living alongside Workday data and workflows. But that expressiveness comes with a cost.

## **The Trust and Governance Surface**


MCP Apps deliberately runs code you didn’t write inside your host. Even with iframe sandboxing, templates, and auditable JSON‑RPC messages, you’ve materially expanded your trust surface compared to a purely declarative UI. In consumer tooling, you might treat that as a straightforward security problem. Where we work, in enterprise systems of record, payroll, financial close, compliance, that’s not enough.


You need to answer:


- How does this embedded app participate in *existing* approval and audit flows?
- How do you ensure permission checks and data access match the semantics you enforce for humans and services?
- What happens when the embedded UI wants to trigger side‑effects in systems where “almost right” is wrong?


The MCP spec acknowledges this with layered defenses and explicit consent semantics. In a Workday style stack, you’d want to go further: plug these experiences into the same governance frameworks you use for core workflows, not run them in parallel.


## **Interoperability and Consistency**


On paper, interoperability is good. MCP Apps are already supported by multiple hosts and are being adopted across a wide set of vendors.


The tradeoff is **visual and behavioral consistency** :


- An HTML widget tuned for one host’s theme may look off, or outright wrong in another.
- The host can’t natively enforce its own design system or accessibility semantics inside the iframe.
- Bridging semantics like keyboard shortcuts, screen readers, or responsive layout becomes a per integration concern.


In many ways, MCP is the right model when:


- You’re integrating with sophisticated partners that already have a strong UI.
- Users expect to “be in” that application’s interface, just in a new context.
- You’re willing to accept a larger governance and UX integration boundary in exchange for richness.


In Workday Agent Factory terms: this is closer to the “bring your own studio” end of the spectrum.


## **A2UI: Agents Describe Intent, Clients Enforce the Rules**


[Google’s A2UI specification](https://github.com/google/A2UI) takes the opposite stance. Instead of shipping executable UI, agents emit **declarative JSON** describing the interface they want: cards, inputs, tables, charts, buttons, date pickers, and so on. The client decides how to render each component using its own trusted library. The payload is essentially a flat list of component descriptions:


- Each component has a type, data bindings, and interaction hooks.
- Components refer to each other via IDs in an adjacency list style graph.
- The host maintains a catalog of allowed component types and maps each type to a concrete widget implementation in React, SwiftUI, Angular, Flutter, whatever your stack uses.


The agent never touches the DOM. It never ships code. It only expresses **intent over a finite palette** . This maps almost perfectly to how you’d want durable agentic systems to behave in an enterprise:


- **The host owns the palette:** what can be rendered, how it looks, how it behaves, which accessibility and security policies apply.
- **The agent owns composition:** which components to place, how to connect them, what data to bind, when to show or hide.

## **Designed for Cross‑Boundary Agents**


A2UI’s design explicitly targets multi‑agent, cross‑org scenarios: an orchestrator inside your environment calls into remote sub agents owned by other teams or vendors. In those situations, allowing remote agents to inject arbitrary UI code into your application is a non‑starter. With A2UI:


- Remote agents describe *what* they want rendered.
- Your client decides *how* it shows up, using components that already meet your compliance, design, and accessibility bars.
- The entire “attack surface” reduces to the set of component types you explicitly trust.


For a platform like Workday, this lines up with the posture that AI should operate inside the same rails as HR and Finance systems, not alongside them. The platform remains the system of record and system of action; agents are guests who get to compose with the furniture you’ve already bolted down.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## **Streaming and Portability**


A2UI’s JSON structure is intentionally friendly to LLM generation:


- Models can stream components incrementally, enabling progressive rendering. Users see real UI appear as the agent thinks.
- The same payload renders natively across platforms, as long as each client implements the agreed component catalog.


If you imagine Workday surfaces: web, mobile, embedded side panels, external tools connected via[Sana](https://www.workday.com/en-us/artificial-intelligence.html?_gl=1*pj22mp*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..&gclid=EAIaIQobChMI0LncpLr7lQMVTwGtBh1v-wfKEAAYASAAEgLSwfD_BwE&gclsrc=aw.ds&gbraid=0AAAAADgCFKfvFty7xhO7Ax2S8xLfmU-OA) , you can see why this matters. You want:


- One semantic description of the interface.
- Native, consistent experiences everywhere it appears.
- A single set of policies around what components exist and how they’re allowed to behave.


## **The Expressiveness Ceiling**


Of course, there’s a bound:


- If your catalog supports Chart, DataTable, and ActionPanel, agents can build surprisingly rich workspaces.
- If you don’t define 3DModelViewer, no agent can render one without a host update.
- Extensibility exists, you can map new server side component types to host implementations, or even include iframes for legacy content, but that requires deliberate client work.


In other words: **A2UI is only as powerful as your palette.** For teams like Agent Factory, that’s not a bug; it’s the point. It forces you to invest in the component library, contracts, and governance layer instead of over‑indexing on prompt hacks and brittle UI generation.


## **Flexibility vs Safety: Choosing Who Holds the Brush**


Taken together, MCP Apps and A2UI encode a core architectural tension:


- **MCP Apps** : the server holds the brush. It shows up with its own UI stack. The host’s job is to sandbox, broker messages, and draw a few hard lines around side effects.
- **A2UI** : the host holds the palette. The agent is allowed to arrange known pieces in new ways, but never to introduce new primitives without buy‑in.


If you strip away the spec names and acronyms, the real question is: For each UI surface your agent can touch, who do you trust to define the experience — *and what does that imply for your governance model?*


From a Workday perspective, where you operate at the heart of HR and Finance, this maps pretty cleanly:


- For **first‑party and tightly governed experiences** that operate directly on payroll, close, or compliance workflows, you want A2UI‑style declarative control. The system of record owns the palette; agents compose within it.
- For **deep partner integrations** where users expect a full fidelity partner UI, analytics notebooks, design tools, specialized vertical apps — MCP‑style embedded apps are a fit, as long as they plug into existing controls rather than bypass them.


Most serious platforms will need both. The mistake is to treat them as interchangeable.

## **The Agent Canvas: Where Generative UI Comes to Life**


So far, you can imagine all of this living inline in chat. Ask a question, get back cards and widgets. For light use cases, that’s fine. But if you’ve ever watched a finance leader, HRBP, or operations manager actually work, you know chat is the wrong workspace:


- It’s linear and append‑only.
- Past outputs scroll away.
- You can’t compare two artifacts side by side.
- You can’t incrementally refine a view without spamming the thread.


Chat is a conversation medium, not a working medium. Enter the **agent canvas** .


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Think of the canvas as a persistent, spatially organized work surface, often a side panel or full‑screen mode, where generative components live *outside* the chat timeline:


- A dashboard generated for Monday’s standup is still there on Tuesday.
- An analyst can keep three chart variants visible while exploring drivers.
- A recruiter can review candidate summaries, job details, and suggested actions in a single layout, all editable.


It has a few important properties:


- **Persistence.** Components don’t disappear into the scrollback. They’re stateful artifacts you can return to, share, and evolve.
- **Composition.** Multiple components from multiple tools or sub‑agents can coexist: tables, charts, forms, explanation panels, action launchers.
- **Editability.** Users can filter, rearrange, override, and augment what the agent produced, without dropping back to raw prompts.
- **Context handoff.** The canvas becomes a shared memory between human and agent; every interaction is new context for the next step.


From an implementation perspective:


- MCP Apps power canvases by letting the host arrange embedded iframes spatially and broker messages.
- A2UI powers canvases by letting the host own layout and state management while agents stream new components into the graph.


From an enterprise-AI perspective, the canvas is where the idea of “AI as a teammate” becomes tangible. It’s where agents can actually *do work* , assemble views, propose actions, and help users drive outcomes, while staying grounded in the same permissions, approvals, and audit trails that core workflows use.


## **Enterprise Constraints: Systems of Record and Rails**


So far, nothing about MCP Apps or A2UI inherently cares whether you’re building for a side project or for a system that moves real money. Enterprise environments like Workday add constraints that change the calculus:


- **Systems of record.** Agents are not playing with copies of data; they’re sitting on HR and Finance primitives where “almost correct” isn’t acceptable.
- **Deterministic foundations.** Underlying business processes are deterministic by design. They start, end, and leave auditable traces. Agents have to fit into that world, not erode it.
- **Existing governance frameworks.** Approval chains, audit trails, policy engines, and compliance dashboards already exist. You can’t bolt on a separate governance universe just for agents.


These constraints push you toward a few design principles:


- Treat **UI architecture as a governance decision** , not just a UX one. Choosing MCP vs A2UI is deciding who’s responsible for correctness and who has to prove it.
- **Plug agents into existing controls.** Whether you embed partner UIs or render native components, permission checks, logging, and approvals should use the same rails you use for humans and services.
- **Bias toward declarative contracts.** The more semantics you can encode in component types, schemas, and interaction contracts, the easier it is to evaluate, test, and reason about agent behavior over time.


This is very close to how durable agent systems are already being built:[thin agent layers on top of thick, well governed foundations](https://medium.com/workday-engineering/by-zeke-miller-director-machine-learning-engineering-at-workday-b5a8cbd55c97) .

## **What This Means for Builders**


If you’re a staff or senior engineer in this space, here’s the frame to use when you sit down to make decisions about your own architecture.


**1. Design the Palette Like You’d Design a Platform:** Your generative UI is only as competent as the palette you give it. Invest in:


- A well‑factored component library that covers the real tasks in your domain: not “Button” and “Card,” but “HeadcountTrend,” “ApprovalQueue,” “VarianceTable,” “ContractSummary,” and so on.
- Clear contracts for each component: required/optional fields, data types, allowed actions, and failure semantics.
- Strong defaults for styling, accessibility, and behavior so you can render the same semantic component across devices and hosts without rewriting logic.


If you do that well, A2UI‑style declarative generation becomes far more powerful than it looks on paper.


**2. Choose Who Holds the Brush Based on Trust:** Don’t start with the spec; start with the trust relationship:


- If the UI source is **your own team or a tightly governed partner** , and users expect the full experience of that app inside your canvas, MCP Apps are a reasonable choice, provided you integrate them into existing governance, not bolt them on.
- If the UI source is a **remote agent, vendor, or internal team you treat as untrusted** , or if the surface touches critical systems of record, favor A2UI‑style declarative contracts where the host owns execution and enforcement.


This isn’t just about safety; it’s about being able to explain your system and stand behind it when something goes wrong.


**3. Build for Chat and Canvas from Day One:** It’s tempting to ship chat + inline cards first and treat the canvas as “phase two.” In practice:


- Your first serious users will immediately push past what chat can support.
- Without a canvas, every new workflow becomes another bespoke thread of prompts and replies, impossible to reason about or govern at scale.
- Architecting your UI contracts and orchestrations with a canvas in mind from the beginning makes it far easier to evolve from “assistant” to “teammate.”


You don’t have to launch the full canvas experience on day one. But you should make sure your generative UI contracts aren’t blocked on a linear chat thread forever.


**4. Watch (and Shape) the Convergence:** Both MCP Apps and A2UI are moving fast. Early frameworks are already experimenting with transports that support both. The likely end state looks less like “MCP vs A2UI” and more like:


- A **core declarative layer** that most agents use for 80–90% of interfaces.
- A **narrow lane for fully embedded apps** , used sparingly for partners who genuinely need full control over their UI and are willing to meet your governance bar.

If you’re building from within an enterprise, you have a chance to shape that convergence rather than consume it. The decisions you make about palettes, contracts, and rails will determine how far agents can go in your domain. We’re at the point where the UI can’t be treated as a static artifact any more than the model can. Interfaces are going to be composed fresh for every user, every task, every context, often by agents, not humans.


Our job, especially in environments where people and money actually move, is to make sure those interfaces are grounded in systems we can trust: governed components, deterministic workflows, and rails that let agents operate safely at the heart of the business. The models will keep getting better. The teams that win are the ones who design a palette worth painting with, and who are clear about who’s allowed to hold the brush.
